summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of the Scottish Parliament, covering its reserved and devolved powers, question time procedures, its Holyrood building in Edinburgh, and its committee and bill systems. It also summarises the history leading to devolution, including the 1997 referendum and the Scotland Act 1998, and the chamber's seating and the West Lothian question.
one_line: Overview of the Scottish Parliament's powers, procedures, committees, bill process, Holyrood building, and devolution history.
key_facts: Reserved matters include abortion, broadcasting policy, defence and national security, employment, foreign policy and relations with Europe, and social security.
The Scottish Parliament building in Holyrood, Edinburgh, was designed by Spanish architect Enric Miralles in partnership with RMJM.
Queen Elizabeth II opened the new Scottish Parliament building on 9 October 2004.
The Scottish Parliament can alter income tax in Scotland by up to 3 pence in the pound.
Following a referendum in 1997, the Scotland Act 1998 convened the current Parliament, whose first meeting took place on 12 May 1999.
Kilbrandon Commission was set up in 1969 by Harold Wilson's Labour government and published its report in 1973, recommending a directly elected Scottish Assembly.
First Minister's Question Time takes place between 12 p.m. and 12:30 p.m. on Thursdays when Parliament is sitting.
The debating chamber has 131 seats: 129 for elected MSPs and 2 for the Scottish Law Officers, who cannot vote.
The Bureau consists of the Presiding Officer and one representative from each political party with five or more seats in the Parliament.
Private Bill Committees have considered the Edinburgh Tram Network, the Glasgow Airport Rail Link, the Airdrie-Bathgate Rail Link and extensions to the National Gallery of Scotland.
Acts of the Scottish Parliament begin with a phrase stating the bill was passed by the Parliament and received royal assent on specified dates, rather than a conventional enacting formula.
After a bill is passed, a 4-week period must elapse before royal assent, during which the Law Officers can refer the bill to the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom.
In the 2011 election the SNP won a majority, the first time a party had commanded a parliamentary majority in the Scottish Parliament; Iain Gray retained East Lothian by 151 votes.
The West Lothian question refers to Scottish MPs at Westminster voting on England-only domestic legislation, which led to a new 'veto' for English MPs after the 2015 UK election.
